cues.text: In 1297, a priest of Gerona , in Catalonia, was celebrating Mass when he found himself privately troubled by doubt.
He doubted whether the Host he was consecrating truly became the Body of Christ, yet confided this to no one.
He continued the Mass as though nothing were wrong.
A Host That Could Not Be Swallowed
When the priest came to receive Communion himself, tradition holds, the Host had transformed inside his own mouth into living, bleeding flesh.
It had grown to a size and consistency he could not swallow at all; forced to remove it, he wrapped it in a cloth rather than complete the rite as he had begun it.
A nun present at the Mass is said to have recovered the transformed relic from the priest.
Shaken by what had happened in his own mouth, he confessed openly the doubt that had troubled him during the consecration—a private struggle made suddenly, and involuntarily, public.
The relic of the transformed Host remained venerated in Gerona for well over six centuries, drawing pilgrims.
It appeared among accounts collected by later chroniclers of the region's Eucharistic devotions, until widespread religious violence destroyed it during the Spanish Civil War in 1936.
Though the physical relic no longer survives, the account of Gerona's doubting priest remains part of the documented record of Spain's medieval Eucharistic traditions.
It is one more instance, alongside Ivorra and others, of an unfeigned private doubt met, in the memory the Church has kept, not with condemnation.
It was met instead with a sign that left the doubter more certain than before he had ever questioned.
